config.title: Valid Parentheses

intro.title: Valid Parentheses
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that checks if a given string of parentheses is valid. A valid string has every opening parenthesis closed in the correct order, like '()[]{}'. You will learn to use a stack data structure to track opening brackets as you iterate through the string. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, arrays (acting as a stack), and loops. This exercise will help you practice lesson-solving with common data structures and control flow.
intro.usecase: The parentheses validation algorithm is essential in code editors and IDEs, where it automatically checks for balanced brackets in real-time as developers write code. This pattern appears in form validation systems that verify nested structures like JSON configuration files or mathematical expressions in calculators. It's also critical in template engines and markup parsers that need to ensure properly closed HTML/XML tags or template directives. Understanding this algorithm helps developers build robust validation for any system requiring balanced delimiter checking.

objectives: Implement a function that determines if a string of parentheses is valid.
Apply a stack data structure to track opening parentheses.
Construct a mapping of closing to opening parentheses for validation.
Manipulate the stack by pushing and popping elements based on character checks.
Control the algorithm's flow to handle edge cases like empty strings and mismatched pairs.
Initialize and return a boolean result indicating the string's validity.
Integrate the validation function into a simple test harness to verify correctness.

content.body: Have you ever wondered how code editors know if your parentheses are balanced? In this lesson, we'll solve the classic Valid Parentheses lesson. You'll learn to use a stack data structure to check if opening and closing brackets match correctly.
content.title: Let's begin

content.body:
• Explain why a stack is perfect for matching parentheses
• Implement a stack-based solution in JavaScript
• Identify when to use stack vs queue for different lessons
• Handle edge cases like empty strings and mismatched brackets
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you're stacking plates in a cafeteria. You can only take the top plate off the stack. Now look at this string: '({[]})'. How would you check if every opening bracket has a matching closing bracket in the right order? Try tracing it with your finger.
content.title: Think about it

content.body: You probably noticed that the last opening bracket you see needs to match the first closing bracket you encounter. This 'last in, first out' pattern is exactly how a stack works!
content.title: What you noticed

content.body: For short strings like '()', you might check manually. But what about code with hundreds of brackets? We need a systematic approach that works for any length. The stack gives us that systematic checking method.
content.title: Why it matters

content.body: Think of opening brackets as plates you stack up. When you see a closing bracket, it must match the top plate (the most recent opening bracket). If it matches, you remove that plate. If all plates are removed by the end, the brackets are balanced.
content.title: Stack thinking
content.visualMetaphor: Stack: pile of plates. Queue: people in a line.

content.body: We'll use a stack (array in JavaScript) to track opening brackets. As we read the string left to right: push opening brackets onto the stack, and when we see a closing bracket, check if it matches what's on top of the stack. If everything matches and the stack is empty at the end, the parentheses are valid.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Create an empty stack (array)
2. Loop through each character in the string
3. If it's an opening bracket ('(', '{', '['), push it onto the stack
4. If it's a closing bracket, check if the stack is empty (invalid) or if the top doesn't match (invalid)
5. If it matches, pop from the stack
6. After the loop, if the stack is empty → valid, otherwise → invalid
content.title: Step-by-step logic

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called isValid that takes one parameter 's' (the string of brackets). Return true for now.
steps.hint: Remember function syntax: function name(parameter) { return value; }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function skeleton.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure your function is called 'isValid' and takes parameter 's'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create: function isValid(s) { return true; }

steps.title: Create the stack
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create an empty array called 'stack'. This will serve as our stack data structure.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! The stack is ready to track opening brackets.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Did you declare 'stack' as a constant array?
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: const stack = []; inside the function.

steps.title: Loop through characters
steps.instruction: Add a for loop to iterate through each character in the string 's'. Use a traditional for loop or for...of.
steps.hint: Try: for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) or for (let char of s)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we can examine each bracket.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Make sure your loop goes through all characters of 's'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) { }

steps.title: Handle opening brackets
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, check if the current character is an opening bracket ('(', '{', or '['). If it is, push it onto the stack.
steps.hint: Use an if statement with logical OR: if (char === '(' || char === '{' || char === '[')
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Opening brackets are now being stacked up.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your condition. It should match '(' OR '{' OR '['.

steps.title: Handle closing brackets and final check
steps.instruction: Add an else clause to handle closing brackets. Check if the stack is empty (return false) or if the top doesn't match (return false). If it matches, pop from stack. After the loop, return whether stack is empty.
steps.hint: Use stack[stack.length-1] to peek at top, and stack.pop() to remove. Create a mapping object: const pairs = { ')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '[' }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the complete stack solution!
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your closing bracket logic. Remember to: 1) check if stack empty, 2) check if top matches, 3) pop if matches.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: if (stack.length === 0 || stack[stack.length-1] !== pairs[char]) return false; stack.pop();

content.body: You've successfully implemented the Valid Parentheses algorithm using a stack! Remember: stacks are perfect for matching lessons where order matters (last in, first out). Queues would be wrong here because they're first in, first out—like a line of people. The cost of push/pop on a stack is O(1), making this solution efficient. Try testing your function with '()[]{}', '(]', and '([)]' to see it in action!
content.title: Well done!
